name: Cruelty to nonlivestock animals (torture)
conduct: Torturing an animal, or killing or causing serious bodily injury to it in a cruel manner. The current statute permits intentional, knowing, reckless or criminally negligent conduct. Criminal negligence was added effective September 1, 2025; conduct with any element before that date requires the earlier law, which did not include that mental state. Covered animals include domesticated creatures, stray or feral cats/dogs and previously captured wild creatures, but exclude uncaptured wild creatures and livestock. Custody concerns care and control, not only ownership. Generally accepted and otherwise lawful fishing, hunting, trapping, wildlife/depredation control and livestock husbandry/agriculture practices are statutory exceptions; an activity label alone does not establish lawfulness. Bona fide scientific experimentation is a defense. Reasonable fear of bodily injury to a person from a statutorily defined dangerous wild animal is a defense. For alleged criminal negligence only, actual discharge of duties as a licensed veterinarian or a person assisting that veterinarian is a defense.
penalty: Third-degree felony: ordinarily two to ten years in prison and a possible fine up to $10,000. One prior conviction under §42.092(b)(1), (2), (7) or (8), or under §42.09 changes this branch to Second-degree felony: ordinarily two to twenty years in prison and a possible fine up to $10,000. Other repeat-offender/deadly-weapon findings require their own statutory analysis; no prior is assumed. A conviction also creates the five-year animal-possession/control restriction in §42.107; that is a separate offense, not an extension of this custody term.

name: Cruelty to nonlivestock animals (kill or poison or injure)
conduct: Without the owner’s effective consent, killing, administering poison to, or causing serious bodily injury to an animal. The current statute permits intentional, knowing, reckless or criminally negligent conduct. Criminal negligence was added effective September 1, 2025; conduct with any element before that date requires the earlier law, which did not include that mental state. Covered animals include domesticated creatures, stray or feral cats/dogs and previously captured wild creatures, but exclude uncaptured wild creatures and livestock. Custody concerns care and control, not only ownership. Generally accepted and otherwise lawful fishing, hunting, trapping, wildlife/depredation control and livestock husbandry/agriculture practices are statutory exceptions; an activity label alone does not establish lawfulness. Bona fide scientific experimentation is a defense. Reasonable fear of bodily injury to a person from a statutorily defined dangerous wild animal is a defense. For alleged criminal negligence only, actual discharge of duties as a licensed veterinarian or a person assisting that veterinarian is a defense. Subsections (b)(2) and (b)(6) also have specific defenses for an animal discovered on the actor’s property in the act of or after injuring/killing livestock or damaging crops and killed/injured at that discovery, and for qualifying public-servant or electricity/natural-gas work. These are not blanket defenses to other cruelty branches.
penalty: Third-degree felony: ordinarily two to ten years in prison and a possible fine up to $10,000. One prior conviction under §42.092(b)(1), (2), (7) or (8), or under §42.09 changes this branch to Second-degree felony: ordinarily two to twenty years in prison and a possible fine up to $10,000. Other repeat-offender/deadly-weapon findings require their own statutory analysis; no prior is assumed. A conviction also creates the five-year animal-possession/control restriction in §42.107; that is a separate offense, not an extension of this custody term.

penalty: Class A misdemeanor: ordinarily up to one year in jail, a fine up to $4,000, or both. Two prior convictions under §42.09, two under §42.092, or one under each changes this branch to State jail felony: ordinarily 180 days to two years in state jail and a possible fine up to $10,000. name: Attack on assistance animal (direct attack)
conduct: Intentionally, knowingly or recklessly attacking an assistance animal. Assistance animal has the specific Human Resources Code §121.002 definition, including required special training/equipment; not every pet or emotional-support animal qualifies. Custody includes responsibility for care and control regardless of ownership. The grade follows the actual attack, injury or death, not merely the intended outcome.
penalty: Class A misdemeanor: ordinarily up to one year in jail, a fine up to $4,000, or both. Repeat-offender or other statutory findings require separate analysis. The court must order owner restitution under §42.091(d) for related veterinary/medical bills, replacement or retraining costs and other reasonably incurred expenses. A conviction also creates the five-year animal-possession/control restriction under §42.107.
